   Malaysia expects tourism fallout from Indonesia haze
 Sign up now: Get insights on the biggest stories in Malaysia
 Haze has disrupted flights and obscured some of Malaysia’s best-known attractions.
 PHOTO: EPA
 Published   Oct 21, 2026, 08:45 AM
 Updated   Oct 21, 2026, 12:17 PM
 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise Malaysia’s tourism sector is facing fewer bookings and cancellations as haze from Indonesia’s wildfires covers major cities and attractions.
 Air pollution has disrupted flights, closed some schools and raised health worries, with Kuala Lumpur, Singapore and Jakarta among the world’s 10 most-polluted cities, says IQAir.
 The haze could cost millions of ringgit in lost revenue, just as Malaysia aims for 47 million visitors in 2026 under its Visit Malaysia 2026 campaign.
 AI generated
 KUALA LUMPUR – Australian tourist Cathy Hamilton was experiencing pangs of regret about her visit to Malaysia as she struggled to take pictures of the haze-shrouded Petronas Twin Towers. 
 “I tried to get some nice photos of the Twin Towers, Merdeka 118 and other scenery, but I couldn’t get good shots as they were all clouded by the haze,” said the Sydney native, who also struggled to breathe as smoke from Indonesia’s wildfires choked the region. 
 Had it not been for the ICU Asian Cheerleading Championships her daughters attended during the weekend, she probably would have cancelled her trip, Hamilton said earlier this week.
 She is not the only tourist reconsidering Malaysia as haze blankets the country.
 Tourism operators are experiencing fewer bookings for this time of year – and even cancellations – as smog disrupts flights, obscures some of the country’s best-known attractions and threatens a key driver of the South-east Asian economy. 
 Kuala Lumpur, Singapore and Jakarta were listed among the world’s 10 most-polluted major cities on Oct 20, according to live rankings from air-quality monitoring company IQAir. The bad air prompted schools to close in some parts of Malaysia. 
 Inbound tour operators are reporting cancellations for November and fewer group bookings, while overseas travel agents are seeking updates on air quality, according to Malaysian Inbound Tourism Association president Mint Leong.
 The slowdown comes as Malaysia targets 47 million visitors in 2026 under its extended Visit Malaysia 2026 campaign. The country recorded 28.8 million international visitors in the first eight months of 2026, according to Tourism Malaysia.
 The Ministry of Tourism did not respond to queries on the effect of the haze on the sector.
 “The loss of revenue could run into the millions” of ringgit, Leong said.
 International visitors spent RM124.8 billion (S$39.2 billion) in the country in 2025 versus RM112.1 billion by domestic tourists, Department of Statistics data show.
 Tourism-related industries generated RM323 billion in economic value in 2025, equivalent to 15.9% of gross domestic product (GDP). Economic activity directly attributable to tourism spending accounted for 6.8% of GDP.
 Despite the hazy conditions, some tourists on Oct 19 were thronging Kuala Lumpur’s Chinatown in search of bargains, although vendor Wong Mei said there had been a drop in customers in October.
 “Fewer people have come out in the last two weeks,” the 62-year-old handbag seller, said, blaming the decline on the haze.
 James Wheatley, a tourist from Britain, said the pollution was not deterring his group’s visit to Malaysia.
 “We just arrived yesterday and will stay until Oct 27. The haze isn’t too bad and we’re adapting to it,” the 60-year-old said as he sampled local fruit at a roadside stall. “Had we known, we would have delayed our trip, but we’re already here.” Bloomberg
